title: Is Walmart the Safest Stock to Own if the Tech Sell-Off Gets Worse?
detail:
Is Walmart the Safest Stock to Own if the Tech Sell-Off Gets Worse?
Dave Kovaleski, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 31, 2026 at 10:50 AM CDT 4 min read
WMT
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Many investors have historically flocked to the safety of consumer staples stocks like Walmart (NASDAQ: WMT) during market downturns or economic slowdowns.

Over the years, Walmart stock has outperformed the market during corrections, bear markets, periods of high inflation, and challenging economic environments because of its lower prices. It gets more foot traffic as shoppers look for deals, pulling in both its traditional budget-conscious shoppers and higher-income consumers who don't want to overpay.

Image source: Getty Images.

If you look at the last bear market in 2022, when inflation was running rampant, Walmart stock was only down 2% compared to the 19% drop in the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) and the 33% decline in the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC).

In 2008, Walmart stock rose 18% while the S&P 500 was off 38% and the Nasdaq fell 40%. And in 2002, when the S&P 500 dropped 23% and the Nasdaq fell 31%, Walmart stock was only down 12%.

Since the Nasdaq closed at an all-time high of 27,599 on Oct. 6, the tech-heavy index has been down about 4%, to roughly 26,470.

Walmart, on the other hand, has been surging in October, up 9% since Sept. 30. The rally has boosted Walmart's year-to-date return to 13% after a summer swoon.

Are investors once again making a flight to safety during a tech sell-off? And are they right to pick Walmart as the safest defensive stock to own? That's debatable.

Big value, big valuation

Walmart is typically a great defensive play, but it's not that great in this particular market. It has had a strong run over the past three-plus-year bull market, continuing its market-beating performance from 2022.

It has averaged a total annualized return of about 32% over the past three years, beating both the Nasdaq Composite and the S&P 500. It successfully pivoted during this period to appeal to a higher-income clientele through investments in its stores, inventory, and online shopping to improve the overall consumer experience.

At the same time, its main rival, Target (NYSE: TGT), had been struggling to attract customers amid higher prices, among other issues, during the bull market. Walmart was able to take some market share from Target, particularly among higher-income shoppers.

But with that success comes a high valuation. Walmart is trading at around 43 times earnings, which is well above its 10-year average of 32. Its forward P/E is 36, but that's still above its long-term average.

title: Costco Is Up 19% in 2026 as It Reinvests Tariff Refunds “to Give Value Back to Our Members”

Costco Is Up 19% in 2026 as It Reinvests Tariff Refunds “to Give Value Back to Our Members”

COST
WMT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Costco Is Up 19% in 2026 as It Reinvests Tariff Refunds "to Give Value Back to Our Members" ©Erik Mclean from Pexels and Leung Cho Pan via Canva
Key Takeaways

Costco shares rose 1.6% Friday to $1,012 and are up 19% in 2026, as September net sales climbed 13% to $30.02 billion.

Fiscal Q4 EPS of $6.75 included a $0.15 one-time benefit from $184 million of tariff refunds, most of which Costco reinvested into lower prices.

Membership fee income growth slowed to 7.3% in Q4, and the stock trades at 44.4x forward earnings with only 5.5% upside to the Street's target.

The November 4 October sales report and December 10 Q1 results will show whether comps stay in double digits.

Costco Wholesale (COST:NASDAQ) got a windfall and handed most of it back to shoppers. That's about as Costco as it gets.

The warehouse club collected $184 million in tariff refunds in its fiscal fourth quarter and used most of it to cut prices on produce, meat, beverages, home furnishings and hardware. Walmart (WMT:NASDAQ) has said it will use billions of dollars in its own refunds to keep prices low, so the value fight just got fresh ammunition.

CEO Ron Vachris said Costco reinvested the money "to give value back to our members."

Investors like the approach. Shares closed Friday at $1,012, up 1.6% on the day and 19% this year.

Refunds flattered a strong quarter

Fiscal fourth-quarter results were solid before any help:

Net sales rose 11.2% to $93.9 billion.

EPS of $6.75 beat estimates and rose 15%, including a $0.15 one-time refund benefit.

Digitally enabled comparable sales jumped 19.5%.

Excluding the refund, EPS still grew 12.4%. September kept the pace going, with net sales up 13% to $30.02 billion and total comps up 11.4%.

U.S. comps ran 12.5%, or 8% excluding gas and currency, so fuel is doing real work. "Our gas business has had a record year," Vachris said on the call.

Strip out the noise, and earnings keep compounding at a steady clip:

Costco Wholesale (COST): diluted EPS, $, fiscal 2021–2025 (TIKR)

Fiscal 2026 diluted EPS reached $20.76, up from $18.21.

The fee engine is cooling

Membership fees are where Costco makes its real money. They totaled $5.9 billion in fiscal 2026, about half of the $11.7 billion operating profit.

That line is slowing. Fourth-quarter fee income rose 7.3% to $1.85 billion, versus 11% for the full year, as the 2024 fee increase laps. Underneath, the base looks healthy: paid executive members grew 9.4% to 42.3 million, and the U.S. and Canada renewal rate ticked up to 92.3%.

Growth will lean more on new buildings. Costco ended the year with 939 warehouses and plans 33 more in fiscal 2027.

Where does the price reinvestment show up? In a gross margin Costco keeps thin on purpose…

Costco Wholesale (COST): gross margin (%), fiscal 2021–2025 (TIKR)

Fourth-quarter gross margin on net sales slipped about 0.1 point to 11.0%, which is what reinvesting refunds should look like.

title: What Walmart (WMT)'s $6b Warehouse Automation Deal Means For Shareholders

What Walmart (WMT)'s $6b Warehouse Automation Deal Means For Shareholders

Walmart Inc. signed an expanded commercial agreement with Symbotic Inc., committing about US$6b to automate 25 U.S. regional distribution centers and support broader supply chain projects over several years.

This large automation spend signals that Walmart is putting significant capital behind warehouse robotics and e-commerce focused inventory management, with attention on storage density, fulfillment speed, and long term operating cost efficiency.

We will now look at how Walmart's multibillion dollar automation push with Symbotic could influence its earnings mix and investment narrative.

Scan how Walmart's automation push compares with other retailers investing heavily in warehouse tech by reviewing our hand-picked 54 AI infrastructure stocks that is powering the next phase of supply chain efficiency.

Walmart Investment Narrative Recap

To own Walmart, you need to buy into a story where low margin physical retail is gradually complemented by higher margin profit pools such as advertising, marketplace fees, membership and now heavier automation. The Symbotic deal fits that thesis, but it is capital intensive and spreads over years, so the near term impact on results is likely limited.

Right now, the key short term catalyst is whether Walmart can keep e-commerce and digital units solidly profitable while volumes stay strong into the holidays. The biggest risk is that delivery and international e-commerce logistics stay expensive, so even with automation spend, margins on fast shipping and grocery could still feel tight.

The Symbotic agreement sits alongside other moves that speak to the same goal of better economics per customer. One of the clearest is the decision to bundle Walmart+ and Sam's Club Plus memberships for US$120 a year, which ties digital benefits, fuel savings and early access to deals into a single package.

For you as an investor, that membership bundle matters because it leans into recurring, fee based income while strengthening the ecosystem that drives marketplace, advertising and e-commerce usage. The risk is that discounts and perks erode some of that membership profit, especially if competitive pressure on prices and ultra fast delivery intensity remains high.

Walmart's narrative projects US$839.4b revenue and US$29.5b earnings by 2029. This assumes 4.5% yearly revenue growth and an earnings increase of about US$7.4b from current earnings of US$22.1b.

Uncover how Walmart's fair value indicates a 5% potential upside to its current price, which could narrow quickly if Walmart keeps executing on its automation plan.

title: Stock Market Today, Oct. 30: Amazon Misses Revenue and Earnings Expectations
detail:
Stock Market Today, Oct. 30: Amazon Misses Revenue and Earnings Expectations
Will Healy, The Motley Fool

AMZN
^GSPC
^IXIC
WMT
COST

Trading disclosure

Amazon.com (NASDAQ:AMZN), a global e-commerce and cloud platform, closed at $240.35, down 1.41%. The stock fell after premarket results missed revenue and earnings expectations, and analysts trimmed price targets during the session. Investors are watching AWS growth, AI spending, and holiday-quarter sales.
Trading volume reached 103.1M shares, coming in about 153% above its three-month average of 38.3M shares. Amazon.com IPO'd in 1997 and has grown 245,363% since going public.

How the markets moved today

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) fell 2.07% to 7,561, while the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC) dropped 2.86% to 25,437. In e-commerce and cloud computing, sector rival Walmart closed at $123.51, up 1.86%, and Costco Wholesale finished at $1,012.28, up 1.63%, highlighting a split in retail sentiment as Amazon.com absorbed post-earnings pressure.

What this means for investors

Despite the decline in the stock price, Amazon's earnings report indicated steady growth, with net sales rising 12% year over year. This included Amazon Web Services (AWS), which returned 39% annual net sales growth, well ahead of the 20% yearly increase in the year-ago quarter.

Where Amazon fell short was with expectations. Both the $201.9 billion in Q3 revenue and the $1.89 in earnings per share, which amounted to an earnings dip, were below the consensus analyst expectations.

Additionally, Amazon stood firm on its $220 billion capital expenditures (capex) goal for 2026. Such spending has become concerning, leading to sell-offs across the sector amid rising interest rates.

Moreover, a company once known for generating tens of billions of dollars in annual free cash flow had a free cash flow outflow of $42.4 billion over the trailing 12 months.

Nonetheless, despite the negative sentiment surrounding Amazon, investors do not seem as panicked as the initial reactions suggested. Even with the capex, Amazon has about $114 billion in liquidity, suggesting it can afford the investment.

Furthermore, the consumer discretionary stock clawed back most of its losses after it opened 5% below yesterday's closing price. Given Amazon's strength in the AI industry, investors have fewer reasons to be concerned about its state.

2 mega-cap stocks with exciting potential and 1 we avoid

Megacap stocks dominate their sectors and their actions influence economies worldwide. The flip side though is that their sheer size means they have less room for explosive growth as scale works against them.

Sound complicated? With StockStory, it doesn't have to be. Our job is to find you high-quality companies that can win regardless of the conditions. Keeping that in mind, here are two industry titans with attractive long-term potential and one that could be stalling.

One mega-cap stock to sell:
Walmart (WMT)

Market cap: $962 billion

Known for its large-format Supercenters, Walmart (NASDAQ:WMT) is a retail pioneer that serves a budget-conscious consumer who is looking for a wide range of products under one roof.

Why Are We Wary of WMT?

The company has faced growth challenges as its 5.3% annual revenue increases over the last three years fell short of other consumer retail companies

Widely-available products (and therefore stiff competition) result in an inferior gross margin of 24.9% that must be offset through higher volumes

Responsiveness to unforeseen market trends is restricted due to its substandard operating margin profitability

Two mega-cap stocks to watch:
Microsoft (MSFT)

Market cap: $3.94 trillion

Originally named "Micro-soft" for microcomputer software when founded in 1975, Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) is a global technology company that develops software, cloud services, devices, and AI solutions for consumers, businesses, and organizations worldwide.

Why Should You Buy MSFT?

Microsoft is one of the great brands not just in tech but all of business. It produces mission-critical software and bundles it together, resulting in cream-of-the-crop gross margins.

The company's elite unit economics lead to robust profit margins that improve over time. This speaks to the scale advantages and operating efficiency across its diverse portfolio, which spans everything from Office and Azure to Minecraft.

Microsoft has a virtuous cycle of returns. Its dominant market position enables it to generate strong free cash flow, and it reinvests these funds into promising ventures that further strengthen its competitive moat.
